Privacy-focused search engine company DuckDuckGo recently released a new survey revealing how much personal information users share with AI chatbots, and how little the public understands about where these conversations ultimately end up. Below are the details of the survey.

The survey shows AI users share more than they realize

DuckDuckGo today published a survey exploring several privacy issues related to the use of AI chatbots. The survey noted that nearly one-third of users have told AI things they would not share with friends, family, colleagues, or healthcare professionals; among self-described AI enthusiasts, this figure rises to 56%.

DuckDuckGo's survey findings are as follows:

The company said that among approximately 2,000 adult respondents in the United States, 53% did not know or were unsure that most chatbots use conversations for training by default, while only 25% knew that AI conversations could be subpoenaed by law enforcement.

The survey results also showed significant behavioral differences between parents and non-parents: parents or guardians living with their children confide in AI at nearly twice the rate of non-parents. DuckDuckGo noted that "among AI users with children at home, 43% have told AI things they have never shared with anyone," while "among AI users without children at home, this figure drops to 25%."

DuckDuckGo believes that AI companies, through advertising and media exposure, encourage users to treat chatbots as confidants, but in reality these conversations may not be as confidential as users think.

Regarding trust, the survey found that the public has slightly more confidence in large AI companies' ability to protect their data than in the US government's. However, both are subject to considerable skepticism: 39% of respondents said they have no trust at all in large AI companies, and 48% feel the same way about the government.

Finally, DuckDuckGo believes users still have the opportunity to change how they handle AI privacy, especially since chatbot usage habits have not yet fully taken shape:

When we talk about online privacy with search engines and browsers, many people think: 'It's too late, my data has already been leaked.' But the most valuable piece of information you can share with Big Tech is your next question—not the one you asked days, months, or even years ago. So it's never too late to switch to more privacy-focused online services.

The company also reminded users that they can take proactive steps to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer and more transparent data handling policies.
